props.title: The Madness of King George
props.initialSlug: Royal king's mind unravels as nation watches

sections.content: The Madness of King George (1994) brilliantly showcases how mental illness intersects with power and politics through Alan Bennett's razor-sharp adaptation of his own stage play. Nigel Hawthorne's towering performance as George III captures both the king's dignified authority and his devastating descent into what modern doctors believe was porphyria. The film sits alongside other masterful portrayals of British monarchs in crisis, like The King's Speech (2010) and The Queen (2006), but brings unique insight into 18th-century medical practices and power dynamics.

sections.content: Director Nicholas Hytner expertly translates the theatrical source material into pure cinema, using the sprawling halls of England's great houses to emphasize George's isolation and mental deterioration. The film's examination of medical history proves especially fascinating, as primitive "treatments" like blistering and purging highlight the period's limited understanding of mental health. This approach to historical medicine links it to films like Restoration (1995) and The Elephant Man (1980), which similarly explore the often-barbaric evolution of medical science.

The political machinations surrounding the king's illness mirror contemporary power struggles in films like The Death of Stalin (2017) and Vice (2018). As the Prince of Wales schemes to be named Regent, the film reveals how mental health stigma could be weaponized for political gain - a theme that resonates even in modern contexts. movies.title: The Favourite
movies.slug: A darkly comic look at power struggles in Queen Anne's court featuring career-best performances from Olivia Colman, Emma Stone, and Rachel Weisz

sections.content: The film's unflinching look at 18th-century medical practices adds another layer of horror to George's ordeal. Like Mary Shelley (2017) and A Dangerous Method (2011), it shows how scientific understanding evolved through often misguided experimentation. Helen Mirren's Queen Charlotte watches helplessly as doctors essentially torture her husband in the name of treatment, highlighting the emotional cost of medical ignorance.
